title: Rivers of living water (John 7:25–52)
hook: on the great day of the feast he cries: let anyone thirsty come

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukkot, huts with roofs of branches, and a teacher with no famous teacher. Your line was judge not by appearance. What question did you ask? Day six hundred thirteen.

A golden pitcher, a pool, and a procession at dawn. According to Jewish tradition written down in the Mishnah, on the mornings of the Feast of Tabernacles a priest walked down to the pool of Siloam with a golden pitcher, filled it with water, and carried it back up to the temple, with crowds and music. At the altar, he poured the water out. In a dry land waiting for the winter rains, that poured-out water meant something. Now it's the last day of the feast, the greatest day. And in the middle of the crowds, Jesus stands up and shouts.

John writes: "In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink." John notes both things: he stood, and he cried out. Then: "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." Belly is the old, literal word. Here it means the deepest inside of a person, which is why some modern translations say heart. And there's a puzzle here. Whose heart? The sentence can be read two ways. Rivers flowing out of the believer, or rivers flowing out of Jesus himself, for anyone who comes and drinks. Readers have taken it both ways. John explains it himself in the next verse: Jesus was speaking about the Spirit, which those who believed would receive. Notice where we've been. A woman at a well heard about living water. A crowd heard about bread. Now, at a festival of water, Jesus offers rivers. And the crowd splits. Some say he's the prophet. Some say he's the Christ. Others say, the Christ can't come from Galilee. Officers are sent to arrest him, and they come back empty-handed. Why didn't you bring him? Their answer: "Never man spake like this man." And one quiet voice speaks up on the council: Nicodemus, who came by night in chapter three. He asks a fair question: shouldn't we hear a man before judging him? He's beginning to come out of the dark.

Here's the practice: drink water with gratitude. If you have a glass of water near you, hold it. If not, picture one. Settle, and breathe. Think about where this water came from. Rain, a river, pipes under your street, the people who keep them working. Take a slow sip. Feel it go down. Notice that your body needed it, even if you didn't feel thirsty. Then think of one person near you who could use a drink, or a kind word. If you pray, you can give thanks for the water. If you don't, simply give thanks for the glass in your hand. The bell holds the time.
Belly. The old, literal word for the deepest inside of a person: out of it, Jesus said, would flow rivers of living water.
Your line: out of the heart, rivers. Today, every time you drink something, give thanks once, and let one kind word flow out to someone else. Day six hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Christians often read this passage at Pentecost, connecting the rivers of living water with the gift of the Holy Spirit; many also connect it with baptism.

original.note: Greek: belly, the inmost part. Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty image about faith overflowing.
what it means: at a festival where water was poured out at the altar, Jesus offers living water, the Spirit, to anyone thirsty.
what a scholar hears: the Greek can put the rivers flowing from the believer or from Jesus, and readers have taken it both ways.
recall: also the phrase for running water

notes: Water-drawing ceremony from Siloam with a golden flagon: Mishnah Sukkah 4:9 (and 5:1 on the rejoicing). Whether it was done on all seven days, and whether the 'great day' is the seventh or eighth, is debated. Confirm.
Two punctuations of 7:37–38 (believer-centered vs. Christ-centered) both have early church support. Confirm.
'Teachers usually sat to teach' (cf. Luke 4:20, Matthew 5:1): confirm generalization.
Index carry says 'heart'; KJV has 'belly'. Script explains both.
